events.name: 2026 Assam floods

The Hindu reported 98 deaths and more than 155,000 still affected as of 8 August 2026; the Wikipedia infobox lists 100+ deaths and more than 700,000 displaced. Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma ordered door-to-door digital damage assessments. Ongoing as of mid-August 2026.

events.name: 2026 Kenya floods

events.what_happened: Flash floods from the March–May 2026 long rains began on the night of 6–7 March when the Nairobi River burst its banks, killing 23 in the capital that night and disrupting flights at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. The National Police Service updated the nationwide death toll to 112 on 3 April 2026. About 6,953 households were affected and at least 34,765 people displaced by the end of March. The Kenya Meteorological Department had issued a heavy-rain warning on 25 February.

events.what_happened: Abundant snowpack and a rapid melt produced the worst Red River flood since 1826. The river crested at 54.35 feet at Grand Forks on 21 April, overtopping dikes built to a 49-foot NWS forecast. Mayor Pat Owens evacuated more than 50,000 people. A downtown fire burned 11 buildings during the flood. Manitoba's Floodway kept Winnipeg's losses far lower; 28,000 were still evacuated in the province. Total regional damage about US$3.5 billion. events.what_happened: After two weeks of rain that saturated soils and reservoirs, extreme rainfall on 19–20 July 1996 produced the largest overland flood in 20th-century Canadian history in the Saguenay graben. Wikipedia records 10 deaths, 16,000 people evacuated, 488 homes destroyed and 1,230 damaged, and about CA$1.5 billion in damage. Over 8 feet (2.4 m) of water flooded parts of Chicoutimi and La Baie. Post-flood inquiries found the dike-and-dam network protecting Chicoutimi poorly maintained. The surviving petite maison blanche became the symbol of the flood.

events.what_happened: Meltwater from the Alps plus prolonged rain in the Ardennes, northern France and Germany sent the Rhine, Meuse, Waal and IJssel to record winter levels. On 25 January the Meuse peaked at 45.09 m NAP at Itteren and Borgharen and flooded parts of South Limburg. At Lobith the Rhine reached 16.68 m (usual range 7.2–12 m). From 31 January more than 250,000 residents and 1 million animals were evacuated from Gelderland and Limburg — one of the largest peacetime evacuations in Dutch history. The Waal dike at Ochten shifted and was held with sandbags; primary dikes did not breach. The near-disaster launched the Room for the River and Meuse Works programmes.

events.what_happened: Persistent heavy rain from spring into summer 1993 produced a months-long flood on the upper Mississippi and Missouri. NOAA and NWS treat it as one of the most damaging river floods in US history. About 50 people died. Some 54,000 people were evacuated. Damage about $15 billion (1993 USD). Hundreds of levees were overtopped or breached as part of the wider river flood.

events.what_happened: August–September 1988 monsoon floods, with the three major rivers peaking together, inundated about 77,700 km² (52% of Bangladesh) including much of Dhaka. USAID recorded at least 2,379 dead (1,644 officially from the floods and more than 735 from later diarrheal disease) and 45 million affected, of whom 25–28 million were homeless. The Big Thompson River rose in a 30-foot (9.1 m) surge through the canyon at about 15 mph. USGS and Wikipedia record 144 deaths, more than 250 injuries and at least 5 missing. 418 homes, more than 400 vehicles and 152 businesses were destroyed. President Ford designated Larimer County a disaster area. A flash-flood warning was issued hours after flooding began.

Combined with the concurrent famine, some compilations cite much higher totals. About a third of the country was underwater. It is one of the country's named catastrophic monsoon floods of the 20th century.

events.what_happened: After three weeks of monsoon rain, weak Tropical Cyclone Wanda crossed the Queensland coast on 24 January 1974 and dumped 642 mm on Brisbane in 36 hours. The Brisbane River peaked at 6.6 m at the Port Office gauge at 02:15 on 29 January. Sixteen people died (twelve drowned in Brisbane and Ipswich), about 300 were injured, at least 6,700 homes were flooded and about 13,000 properties were affected. Final damage exceeded A$980 million (1974 values). The disaster led to flood-mitigation storage at Wivenhoe Dam and was later named a Q150 Icon of Queensland.

The Susquehanna and tributaries flooded Pennsylvania, New York and surrounding states. NOAA and contemporary accounts treat it as one of the costliest US floods of the 20th century. The US Geological Survey and NWS document more than 100 flood deaths; Wilkes-Barre and Corning were among the hardest-hit cities.

The failed relief effort helped precipitate the Bangladesh Liberation War.

About 70,000 families were left homeless; 6,000 shops were destroyed; millions of books and artworks were damaged. International 'Mud Angels' led the salvage.

The event is the reference disaster that later drove the MOSE mobile-barrier project.

events.what_happened: A severe European windstorm plus a high spring tide drove a North Sea storm surge on the night of 31 January–1 February 1953. Dutch sea defences failed in many places (67 breaches in Zeeland alone). Wikipedia records 2,551 fatalities overall: 1,836 in the Netherlands, 307 on land in England, 19 in eastern Scotland, 28 in Belgium, and more than 230 at sea including the sinking of MV Princess Victoria. events.what_happened: A storm of tropical intensity dumped 229 mm of rain in 24 hours on already saturated Exmoor on 15–16 August 1952. Debris-laden floodwaters cascaded down the East and West Lyn. A debris dam in the upper West Lyn failed and sent a wave through Lynmouth. 34 people died; more than 100 buildings were destroyed or seriously damaged; 28 of 31 bridges were lost; 420 people were made homeless.

events.what_happened: The 1950 Red River flood ran from 15 April to 12 June along the Red River in the Dakotas and Manitoba. Winnipeg was inundated on 5 May (Black Friday). The river reached its highest level since 1861 and flooded more than 1,400 km² of the Red River Valley. An estimated 70,000–100,000 residents were evacuated and four of eleven Winnipeg bridges were destroyed. Wikipedia records 3 deaths in Canada and 5 in the United States. Property losses were estimated at $600 million to $1 billion. The disaster led to construction of the Red River Floodway (Duff's Ditch), completed in 1968.

events.what_happened: Spring snowmelt and rain raised the Columbia to record stages. On 30 May 1948 a railroad embankment that served as Vanport's dike gave way, destroying the wartime city of Vanport — then Oregon's second-largest city — in about an hour. Officially 15 people died; some later estimates are higher. About 18,500 residents were displaced. The city was never rebuilt.

events.what_happened: Nationalist forces breached the Yellow River dikes at Huayuankou in June 1938 to slow the Japanese advance. Immediate drowning deaths are estimated at 30,000–89,000. Professional Chinese sources put total deaths from drowning, famine and plague at 400,000–500,000. About five million civilians lived on inundated land until the dikes were repaired in 1947. The river was diverted south into the Huai system for nearly nine years.

About 70% of Louisville was underwater and 175,000 people left their homes. The disaster drove a comprehensive reservoir and levee program on the Ohio.

The Han flooded 427,000 hectares and drowned about 80,000; more than 30,000 drowned along the Li; 23,000 died when the Jing River dike burst. Property damage is given as $333 million (period USD). Affected provinces included Hubei, Hunan, Jiangxi, Anhui, Jiangsu and Zhejiang.

On 25 August dikes near Gaoyou Lake failed; in Gaoyou County alone 18,000 people drowned. Fatality estimates vary widely, from Li Wenhai’s 422,420 (media-based) to official figures around 2 million including famine and disease, and some Western claims of 3.7–4 million.

The American Red Cross recorded 246 deaths; some later estimates are higher. Hundreds of thousands were displaced. The disaster led to the 1928 Flood Control Act.

events.what_happened: Winter rains over a saturated Seine basin raised the river far above ordinary level. Water entered Paris through sewers, Metro tunnels and saturated soil rather than by overtopping the quays inside the city. The Seine peaked at 8.62 m above normal on 28 January. Thousands were evacuated; residents moved by boat and wooden walkways. No deaths were reported. Damage was estimated at about 400 million francs.

Water spread across an estimated 50,000 square miles (130,000 km²) of the North China Plain. Wikipedia records at least 930,000 deaths; estimates range from about 900,000 to 2 million including famine and disease. About two million people were left homeless. It is among the deadliest floods on record.

events.what_happened: Weeks of rain and mountain snow from November 1861 into January 1862, capped by a warm atmospheric-river storm, produced the largest flood in the recorded history of California, Oregon and Nevada. The Central Valley became an inland sea 250–300 miles long and about 20 miles wide (about 5,000–6,000 square miles). Sacramento was underwater for months; the state government temporarily moved to San Francisco. Wikipedia cites at least 4,000 deaths in California (about 1% of the state population) and about $100 million damage in 1861 USD.

The National Museum of Australia describes it as Australia's deadliest flood. About 80–100 people died, roughly a third of the town's population. The settlement was later rebuilt on higher ground.

events.what_happened: A northwesterly storm on Christmas night 1717 drove a storm surge along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Scandinavia. About 14,000 people drowned. Between Tønder and Emden about 9,000 drowned; the Netherlands had about 2,500 victims. Villages behind the sea dikes in Groningen and East Frisia were devastated. A second storm flood followed in late February.

events.what_happened: A catastrophic North Sea storm tide on 11–12 October 1634 (the Burchardi flood, or second Grote Mandränke) struck the coasts of North Frisia, Schleswig-Holstein and southern Denmark. Dikes failed across the region. The island of Strand was broken apart; Nordstrand and Pellworm remain. Death estimates commonly range from 8,000 to 15,000.

events.what_happened: The All Saints' Flood of 1–2 November 1570 is considered the worst North Sea flood disaster before the 20th century. A surge more than four metres above mean high water overran neglected dikes from Calais to Jutland and Norway. Chroniclers reported that 80 percent of the country was under water; the island of Wulpen in Zeeland was permanently lost. Wikipedia states it was confirmed that the floods drowned 20,000 people and that up to 25,000 deaths can be assumed. Between the Ems and Weser about 10,000 people died. A warning had been issued the morning before — the first documented North Sea flood warning.

events.what_happened: A North Sea storm surge on St. Felix's Day (5 November 1530) breached dikes across Zeeland and Flanders. The town of Reimerswaal was destroyed and never rebuilt as a city. The flood is commonly cited with more than 100,000 deaths and is among the deadliest coastal floods on record in the Low Countries.

events.cause_summary: North Sea extratropical cyclone drove a storm surge that overtopped and breached dikes.

events.name: St. Elizabeth's flood (1421)
events.notes: Deaths left unknown on the pin because sourced estimates span 2,000–10,000. Do not treat as zero.

events.status: Historical. Biesbosch National Park occupies much of the still-flooded land.
events.what_happened: On the night of 18–19 November 1421 a North Sea storm surge broke dikes in the Grote Hollandse Waard. Villages were swallowed and the flood created the freshwater tidal wetlands now known as the Biesbosch. Wikipedia records 2,000–10,000 deaths. Most of the area remained flooded for decades; reclaimed remnants include the island of Dordrecht and the Hoeksche Waard.

events.cause_summary: Prolonged rain after a dry period, associated with a Genoa low, produced runoff the dry soils could not absorb.

events.notes: Total death toll unknown. About 6,000 is the figure commonly cited for the Danube area alone. Do not treat as zero.

sources.label: Wikipedia: List of floods in Europe

events.status: Historical. High-water marks survive at Frankfurt and Hann. Münden.
events.what_happened: The largest recorded river flood in central Europe. After a prolonged dry spell, days of continuous rain following a Genoa low inundated the Rhine, Moselle, Main, Danube, Weser, Elbe, Vltava and tributaries around the feast of St. Mary Magdalene (22 July 1342). Cologne, Mainz, Frankfurt, Würzburg, Regensburg, Passau and Vienna were seriously damaged. Würzburg's Steinerne Brücke was washed away. In the Danube area alone it is believed about 6,000 people perished. Erosion is estimated at more than 13 billion tonnes of soil.
